cards.headline: Written as a quiet protest against the Iraq War
cards.snippet: German-born British composer Max Richter recorded "On the Nature of Daylight" in February 2003, as the US-led invasion of Iraq unfolded. It was written for a string quintet: two violins, two cellos and a viola. Richter conceived the piece as a protest against the war and intended its parent album, The Blue Notebooks (released in 2004), to be anti-war. The record explores how fragile truth is and how beauty persists in a violent world. He has described it as a quiet protest against the loud rhetoric of war.
cards.context: From The Blue Notebooks (2004), for string quintet.

cards.headline: Its use in Arrival cost that film an Oscar category
cards.snippet: Max Richter's "On the Nature of Daylight" appeared in the 2016 film Arrival, and it mattered so much there that it cost the film an Oscar category. The piece already existed before the film, and it was judged too central to the film's emotional impact. As a result, Arrival was ruled ineligible for the Academy Award for Best Original Score. The film had its own score, written by Jóhann Jóhannsson.
cards.context: Arrival (2016) had its own score by Jóhann Jóhannsson.

cards.headline: A silent cinema after the credits rolled
cards.snippet: Nobody got up right away after the movie ended, while this was playing. And I checked: nobody was on their phones or anything. We all needed a minute.
cards.context: Describes the piece's effect on a theater audience.

replies.author: @ZmenitBussler
replies.text:
Same at my theater. 

I was busy wiping my tears and trying to find my heart beat. 

Haven’t felt that way watching a movie in a long time.

replies.author: @Andsmithmustscore12
replies.text: Same. People were still trying to take in those last scenes. Has always been a piece of music that speaks to the heart
